<description>At low magnification, an infiltrative epithelial neoplasm is present with irregular gland-like structures in some areas and more solid sheeted or trabecular growth in others. These tumor cell aggregates are intermingled with abundant fibrous stroma showing a prominent fibroblastic/desmoplastic response, and there is scattered lymphocytic infiltration. Residual ductal-type structures are only focally seen and are largely disrupted, supporting invasive growth. At mid magnification, the tumor is composed of nests and cord-like arrangements with cellular crowding/overlapping and partial loss of polarity. The cells have moderate faintly eosinophilic cytoplasm and pleomorphic hyperchromatic nuclei with increased N:C ratio and coarse chromatin, with occasional nucleoli. The surrounding stroma again shows marked fibrosis with small vessel proliferation, without calcifications or comedo-type necrosis. At high magnification, the stromal compartment remains prominently fibrotic, with only a small amount of inflammatory cell infiltration.</description>
<think>The question asks which structure can be confirmed as the same kind of structure appearing in more than one view. Across low, mid, and high magnification, the fibrous stromal component is repeatedly and consistently described as prominent, with a fibroblastic/desmoplastic response at low power, significant fibrosis at mid power, and prominent stromal fibrosis at high power, so this feature is clearly confirmed across views. In contrast, gland/duct-type structures are mentioned at low magnification as irregular glands and locally present disrupted ducts, but the mid and high magnification descriptions emphasize nests and cords with loss of polarity and do not clearly re-identify a matching gland/duct structure, so a gland/duct structure cannot be confidently confirmed across more than one view. Lymphocytic/inflammatory infiltrate is present at low power as scattered lymphocytes and at high power as a small amount of inflammatory cells, so an infiltrate actually is seen in more than one view, making the option claiming it is not clearly confirmed inconsistent. Therefore, the best fit is the option stating fibrosis is visible in more than one view while a matching gland/duct structure is not clearly confirmed across views.</think>
<answer>A</answer>

<description>At low magnification, the lesion is composed of tumor cells arranged in solid sheets and trabecular patterns, with dense cellular areas separated by fibrous stroma such that the parenchyma-to-stroma proportion is roughly equal. The stroma shows a marked fibroblastic proliferative (desmoplastic) response with scattered lymphocytic infiltration. Native ductal structures are largely disrupted, with only a few residual glandular elements, supporting an invasive growth pattern. At mid magnification, the tumor forms irregular nests and cords with loss of polarity and cellular overlap. The cells have moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, sometimes appearing slightly translucent, and nuclei show variability in size with hyperchromasia, increased N/C ratio, coarse granular chromatin, and occasional prominent nucleoli. The stroma contains sparse small vessels, mild fibrous tissue hyperplasia, and a small amount of inflammatory cell infiltration; no calcifications or comedo-type necrosis are identified. At high magnification, there is marked nuclear pleomorphism with thickened, irregular nuclear membranes, coarse uneven chromatin, and conspicuous eosinophilic nucleoli (often 1–2). Occasional mitotic figures, including atypical forms, are present. The cytoplasm remains mildly eosinophilic without evident secretion or vacuolation, and the surrounding fibrous stroma again shows only a small amount of inflammatory cell infiltration.</description>
<think>The key cross-magnification feature in question is lymphocytic or inflammatory cell infiltration. The low-power view explicitly notes scattered lymphocytes within a desmoplastic stroma. On closer inspection at mid and high power, inflammatory cells are not absent; rather, both levels describe a small amount of inflammatory cell infiltration within the fibrous stroma. However, these higher-power descriptions do not emphasize lymphocytes intermingled with tumor nests and cords, nor do they describe numerous lymphocytes throughout the fields. Therefore, the higher magnifications generally support the presence of some inflammatory infiltrate, but they do not “clearly” corroborate prominent lymphocytes within tumor structures, and they certainly do not indicate a dense infiltrate. Among the options, the best match to this partial/limited corroboration is that low power suggests lymphocytes, while mid/high do not provide a clearly corroborating view of lymphocytes specifically, leaving the implication not definitively resolved across scales.</think>
<answer>C</answer>

<description>At low magnification, the tissue is extensively infiltrated by densely distributed malignant cells forming solid sheets and trabecular/nested architectures separated by prominent reactive fibrous (desmoplastic) stroma. In some areas, atypical gland-like structures are present with disruption of the native ductal architecture, and there is a moderate, patchy lymphocytic infiltrate within the stroma. The nests and cords are repeatedly noted in association with fibrous stroma, and there is explicit absence of definite vascular invasion, arguing against tumor being within vascular/lymphatic lumina. The description does not place these structures within a surface epithelial lining layer, and instead emphasizes disruption of original ductal morphology with only some atypical glandular structures, making a purely luminal location unlikely. The most consistent spatial relationship is that the nests and cords are embedded within fibrous stroma between glandular/ductal structures as part of an invasive carcinoma pattern.</think>

<description>At low magnification, the lesion is composed of densely cellular tumor parenchyma arranged in solid sheet-like and trabecular patterns, with focal atypical gland-like/duct-like structures showing irregular, locally destructive contours. The normal ductal architecture is effaced and replaced by a disordered infiltrative growth pattern. Between tumor cell aggregates there is prominent fibrous stroma with a marked fibroblastic (desmoplastic) proliferation and scattered lymphocytic infiltration. At intermediate magnification, the tumor forms diffuse sheets with loss of polarity, cellular overlapping and piling, and scant pale eosinophilic cytoplasm. Nuclei are enlarged and pleomorphic with hyperchromasia, irregular nuclear outlines, and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. The stroma shows fibrous tissue hyperplasia with small-vessel involvement, scattered calcific foci, and no typical comedo-type necrosis. At high magnification, tumor cells are arranged in irregular nests with striking cytologic atypia: marked nuclear size variation, thickened irregular nuclear membranes, coarse uneven chromatin, prominent eosinophilic nucleoli (sometimes double), and frequent mitotic figures including atypical forms such as multipolar mitoses. Cytoplasm remains scant without obvious keratinization, secretions, or vacuoles. The surrounding stroma is distinctly fibrotic with sparse inflammatory cells, supporting an invasive tumor with a desmoplastic stromal response.</description>
<think>The overall architecture shows replacement of the native ductal system by an infiltrative pattern with irregular nests/sheets and locally destructive contours, which argues against an intraepithelial-only process. The presence of prominent fibroblastic stromal proliferation and stromal fibrosis is characteristic of a desmoplastic response, which is a key histologic correlate of stromal invasion rather than carcinoma in situ. Cytologically, the lesion is high grade, with marked pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, prominent nucleoli, and frequent atypical mitoses, supporting an overt carcinoma rather than a benign papilloma with reactive atypia. Microinvasion would imply only very limited focal stromal invasion, whereas the described widespread invasive growth pattern with extensive desmoplastic stroma and irregular nests across the lesion is more consistent with established invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Therefore, the diagnosis most strongly supported by integrating architecture and cytologic detail is invasive squamous cell carcinoma with stromal desmoplastic response.</think>
<answer>D</answer>

<description>At low magnification, the lesion shows an infiltrative malignant epithelial proliferation composed of irregular glandular/duct-like structures admixed with solid sheet-like areas. The tumor is distributed in a desmoplastic background with prominent fibroblastic stromal reaction, with parenchyma and stroma present in roughly comparable proportions. The overall architecture is disorganized, and there is uneven lymphocytic infiltration within the stroma, supporting a destructive invasive growth pattern rather than a purely intraductal process. At intermediate magnification, there are foci with markedly atypical ductal epithelial proliferation showing crowding, disordered arrangement, and loss of polarity, and central comedo-like necrosis is present; however, these intraductal-type changes are seen in the context of surrounding stromal fibrosis rather than a circumscribed papillary lesion. At high magnification, the tumor is composed of irregular nests and glands of markedly atypical cells with enlarged pleomorphic hyperchromatic nuclei, thickened irregular nuclear membranes, coarse uneven chromatin, and occasional prominent eosinophilic nucleoli. Cytoplasm is scant with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, numerous mitotic figures including atypical forms are identified, and inflammatory cells infiltrate the stroma.</description>
<think>Integrating the architecture across magnifications, the dominant low-power impression is of malignant glands and solid sheets infiltrating through fibrous stroma with a marked desmoplastic (fibroblastic) reaction and a disorganized, destructive growth pattern. That stromal response and the described irregular glandular and solid infiltration argue for invasion rather than confinement within pre-existing ducts. The mid-power findings of intraductal epithelial atypia with loss of polarity and comedo-like necrosis are compatible with high-grade DCIS, but the key discriminator in the question is the presence or absence of destructive growth; here, the infiltrative pattern with desmoplasia supports an invasive carcinoma with an associated in situ component rather than pure DCIS. The high-power cytology shows high-grade features with marked pleomorphism and abundant (including atypical) mitoses, fitting a high-grade invasive ductal carcinoma of no special type. Encapsulated papillary carcinoma and solid papillary carcinoma would be expected to show a circumscribed papillary architecture (often with a capsule for encapsulated papillary carcinoma) rather than irregular infiltrative glands and sheets with desmoplastic stroma, so those options are not supported by the described destructive invasion. Therefore, the best-supported diagnosis is high-grade invasive ductal carcinoma NST.</think>
<answer>B</answer>
